items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: because we was friends from New York. A little small friendship.

ctx.x: So you learned early on the importance of rhythm in New Orleans jazz.

That’s what it is. That’s what you be: a rhythm guitar. You don’t have to play solos. You can play rhythm with Sidney Bechet playing. You still . . . what you see, if that’s what it is, you can see that I’m not in his way. I’m not forcing nothing on him. Just giving him a smooth bed to float on. That’s what jazz is all about. That’s what these people away from here don’t know nothing about. They never will get it. They’ve got another thing. They didn’t know how to swing ’til Louis Armstrong start swinging that…
Why do you think in New Orleans people knew how to swing and in other places they didn’t? Why do you think in New Orleans they could swing so much in music . . .

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: And Dizzy came over and said, "Hello" and everything.

ctx.x: Clarence Profit was doing that basically on the piano. You see, all that stuff was in the air, you know. It was just (?)a question(?) of the time of who would get that bug to do it... Charlie had it out West, Dizzy had it here, and it's something that they come together and they fell right in.
What Charlie out in the West?
